title: Complaint of TE Eliot Lee v. Korean Eastern Presbytery
disposition_detail: The SJC sustained Lee’s complaint and annulled Korean Eastern Presbytery’s decision in whole. It did not order dismissal of the civil lawsuit or remand further proceedings.
first_summary: Lee challenged Korean Eastern Presbytery’s ratification and filing of a civil lawsuit through a commission acting for the local church. The suit sought civil adjudication of ecclesiastical questions, including who was the rightful pastor and who could act as the church’s session. The SJC sustained the complaint and annulled Presbytery’s decision because PCA church courts possess spiritual rather than civil coercive authority.
summary: Lee challenged Korean Eastern Presbytery’s ratification and filing of a New Jersey lawsuit through a commission acting for the local church, seeking civil adjudication of who was the rightful pastor and who could act as the church’s session. The SJC sustained the complaint and annulled Presbytery’s decision in whole. PCA courts have moral and spiritual, not civil coercive, authority and cannot sue to enforce ecclesiastical decisions. The ruling does not prohibit litigation over purely civil matters and did not condemn the commission’s original appointment.

sources.supports: Issues, judgment, disposition, reasons, relief, and limitations for Case 2007-10.

evidence_notes.identity_and_adoption: The combined heading identifies SJC 2007-09 and 2007-10 (printed p. 132, line 13); the majority expressly identifies and decides Case 2007-10 (printed p. 137, lines 168–169), with concurrence recorded at lines 253–257.
evidence_notes.dispute: The issue was KEP’s approval and ratification of commission and executive-committee actions and its civil suit seeking a restraining order and adjudication of ecclesiastical matters (printed pp. 136–137, lines 146–156).
evidence_notes.outcomes_and_reasons: The complaint was sustained and KEP’s decision annulled in whole; the majority held that presbyteries cannot use civil courts to coerce obedience to ecclesiastical decisions (printed pp. 137–140, lines 168–177, 226–251). The informal executive-committee call-around also violated Robert’s Rules (printed p. 138, lines 189–195).
evidence_notes.qualifications: Civil courts remain available for purely civil disputes such as trespass or breach of contract; the commission’s appointment was proper, but acting as HKPC’s session and filing the suit were not (printed p. 138, lines 177–187).
evidence_notes.incorporated_decisions: No decision was incorporated by reference. Prior judgments concerning the commission’s proper appointment were summarized and expressly distinguished from its later actions (printed pp. 136, 138, lines 138–142, 179–187).

source_limits: The source combines Cases 2007-09 and 2007-10 and includes a concurrence. It states no ultimate disposition of the New Jersey litigation and orders no relief beyond annulment for Case 2007-10.

score_reasons.concrete_dispute: Identifies the ratified civil suit and the ecclesiastical questions it sought to adjudicate.
score_reasons.decision: States both sustaining the complaint and annulment in whole without adding ungranted relief.
score_reasons.decisive_reason: Explains the constitutional limit against civil coercion of ecclesiastical authority.
score_reasons.distinctive_value: Preserves both the purely civil-matter exception and the distinction between appointment and later conduct.
score_reasons.fidelity: Separates the adopted majority reasoning from the concurrence and prior rulings.
score_reasons.economy: Retains only facts and qualifications needed to understand the result.

verification_notes: Rechecked the case-specific judgment and majority reasoning. The final summary narrows the civil-court prohibition to enforcement of ecclesiastical decisions, adds the purely civil-matter exception, distinguishes the commission’s proper appointment from its improper later conduct, and avoids implying dismissal of the lawsuit or a remand.
